title: Enraged gunman dies in shootout: `He said he wasn't going back to jail,' friend says
article: When Fred Kirkey told his friends he'd rather die than go back to jail, they didn't think he was serious.
But a looming five-month jail sentence coupled with anger toward his former wife's new love, affected the man more than his friends could tell.

Yesterday, the day he was to start serving the sentence for an impaired driving conviction, Mr. Kirkey smiled and told his parents he'd talk to them in a couple of hours. An hour later, he arrived in a rage at the home of his former wife, Loretta Sayeau.
An eyewitness said he crashed his car into the back of her new boyfriend's vehicle, parked outside the house Ms. Sayeau moved into when she left Mr. Kirkey about a year ago.

The witness, who watched from inside another house on the property, said Mr. Kirkey then jumped out of his car with a gun in his hands. The witness said he fired at least three shots from a long-barrelled gun, either a shotgun or hunting rifle, in the direction of Ms. Sayeau's house. Mr. Kirkey fell to the ground, the witness said, after he shot himself or was hit by a rebounding bullet.

Lorne Dougherty, the deputy fire chief of this small town near Prescott, was at home only a three-minute drive down the road, when his pager went off. Brockville fire dispatch often calls Mr. Dougherty when an ambulance will take more than five minutes to arrive.

But that call from dispatch described the situation only as one of potential suicide. Rushing over to help, Mr. Dougherty drove right into the driveway of the house, with no idea he was heading into the zone of gun fire.
Only in retrospect did the firefighter realize what a neighbour was yelling at him as he walked toward the man he saw lying on the ground. That neighbour was telling him to run and take cover.
"I didn't know he had a gun underneath him," said Mr. Dougherty. "When he got up on his knees and lifted up the gun, that's when I started running."

In his haste to take cover, Mr. Dougherty lost his hand-held two- way radio, but using his cellphone, he called his dispatcher to warn them not to send anymore unarmed emergency personnel. He then asked the driver of a half-ton truck to block one side of the road and he waved away cars driving from the other side.

"I was running out and telling them to get the hell out of there," he said. Then he hid behind a hydro pole. Moments later, when two Grenville OPP cruisers pulled up, he told the officers what he'd seen.

At that point, according to the witness at the window, the officers surrounded Mr. Kirkey and pleaded with him: "Put the gun down! Put the gun down!" Instead, Mr. Kirkey fired it, the witness said. Police fired back, and he fell to the ground again.
"Lordy, I nearly jumped out of my skin,"said June Allen, who lives across from the farm and heard the loud blasts. "I thought \`Good glory be!"
Mrs. Allen thought it might just be a car backfiring.
"I thought whatever it was was passing by, not on the doorstep. Living out here you don't expect it. Maybe if I lived in Toronto."

The More Than Just Babysitting day-care centre sits across the country road from the house. Mr. Dougherty said when he arrived children were not playing outside. The playground remained empty all day while police milled about the farm yard marked off with yellow police tape.
Mr. Kirkey was pronounced dead on arrival at the Brockville General Hospital.
His family, however, is reluctant to believe the man they saw walk out the door this morning suddenly turned suicidal.
"He was fine," his sister Tammy Kirkey said last night. "He said he'd talk to us in a couple of hours. We want some answers."

Questioning the use of deadly force, Mr. Kirkey's family issued a statement through their lawyer, Peter Adams. "The family, who are obviously most affected by this tragedy, have been left almost completely in the dark," Mr. Adams said. "They are searching for the answer as to why their friendly and sober son who leaves in the morning with apparent calm will never return."
The province's civilian Special Investigations Unit dispatched six investigators, including two forensic specialists, to probe Ontario's third fatal shooting involving police this year.

Reached by the Citizen inside the kitchen of a neighbouring house, Ms. Sayeau would not talk about the shooting. She remained calm as she read the police news release describing an exchange of gunfire between police and a suicidal Mr. Kirkey and confirmed that description.
"That's the gist of it," she said.
"He said he wasn't going back to jail," Mr. Kirkey's employer and long-time friend Ian Conklin said.
"Then his ex-wife, she moved a new man in on the weekend, and that aggravated him that much more. He just lost it, I guess."
Mr. Kirkey had done short time in jail before, Mr. Conklin said, for domestic abuse and impaired driving offences.
"He didn't take to jail too well. He's the type of guy who could sleep outside, he likes the outdoors pretty good. He just couldn't stand being locked up."
Mr. Conklin said Mr. Kirkey's world crumbled when Ms. Sayeau, his wife of about eight years, left him about a year ago.
Mr. Kirkey moved in with his parents and turned to the bottle, Mr. Conklin said.
"He drank quite a bit," he said, "but since the split with his girlfriend, he had been drinking a lot more, whisky and beer."
Despite some destructive habits, Mr. Kirkey, 235 pounds of muscle, was for years a valued labourer at the 810-hectare Conklin Farm, where he earned about $400 a week, his boss said.

John Dawson, an area farm-hand, said he wished he'd have been there to talk his close friend out of trouble. Mr. Dawson wanted to give Mr. Kirkey a ride to the courthouse that morning, but couldn't because he had to work.
"I've talked him out of a lot of things -- fighting," he said. "I know he would have listened to me."
Mr. Dawson said Mr. Kirkey was prohibited from owning a gun after an incident in which he had emptied a loaded gun in the parking lot of an area Burger King.
